lessons.title: Splitting Your Cost of Acquisition After a Demerger

children.text: A few months after the Jio Financial Services demerger, thousands of Reliance shareholders sold their JFS shares and opened their broker's tax statement. Many saw a buy price of zero, and a capital gain equal to the entire sale value. Others saw their original Reliance cost still sitting untouched against Reliance alone. Both were wrong. When one share becomes two holdings, your original purchase cost has to be divided between them, using a formula set by tax law, not by market prices. Get it wrong and you either overpay tax or under-report a gain.

body.text: A demerger does not change what you paid. It splits that single cost across two holdings, in the proportion of book value transferred, not market value. The new shares also inherit the parent's purchase date, so your holding period does not restart.

children.text: The Three Tax Rules That Apply
Receiving the shares is not a sale.

Under section 70 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (section 47(vid) of the 1961 Act), the issue of resulting company shares to the parent's shareholders in a qualifying demerger is not treated as a transfer. No capital gains tax arises on the record date.
Your cost is split.

Under section 73 of the 2025 Act (sections 49(2C) and 49(2D) of the 1961 Act), part of the original cost moves to the resulting company's shares, and the parent's cost is reduced by exactly that amount.
Your holding period carries over.

Under section 2(101) of the 2025 Act (section 2(42A) of the 1961 Act), the period you held the resulting company's shares includes the period you held the parent's shares. Listed shares held for more than 12 months qualify as long-term.
The Cost Split Formula

body.latex: \text{Cost of new shares} = \text{Original cost} \times \frac{\text{Net book value of assets transferred}}{\text{Net worth of parent just before demerger}}
body.caption: The ratio is calculated by the company from its audited books. You apply it to your own purchase cost.

body.latex: \text{Revised cost of parent shares} = \text{Original cost} - \text{Cost of new shares}
body.caption: The two costs always add back to exactly what you paid.

children.text: You do not need to calculate the ratio yourself. After a demerger, the parent usually announces the
cost of acquisition apportionment
on BSE and NSE, often as a pair of percentages that add up to 100%.

markDefs.definition: The percentages, announced by the company, in which shareholders should divide the original cost of their parent shares between the parent and the resulting company for tax purposes.

body.label: Reliance Industries and Jio Financial Services cost apportionment
body.context: Reliance announced this split after the 2023 demerger, based on the book value of the financial services undertaking relative to its net worth.

body.title: How a Reliance shareholder's original cost is divided

children.text: Worked Example: Ramesh's Reliance Shares
Ramesh bought 100 Reliance shares at ₹2,000 each, a total cost of ₹2,00,000. On the record date he received 100 JFS shares at 1 for 1.

body.title: Ramesh sells his JFS shares
body.prompt: Fourteen months after buying his Reliance shares, Ramesh sells all 100 JFS shares at ₹300 each. Using his JFS cost of ₹9,360, what is his capital gain, in rupees? Ignore brokerage and other costs.
body.explanation: Sale value = 100 × ₹300 = ₹30,000. Gain = ₹30,000 minus ₹9,360 = ₹20,640. Because his holding period counts from his Reliance purchase 14 months earlier, this is a long-term gain. If his total long-term gains on listed equity for the year stay within ₹1.25 lakh, no tax is payable on it.

body.text: Had Ramesh accepted a broker statement showing zero cost for JFS, he would have reported a ₹30,000 gain instead of ₹20,640. Had he kept the full ₹2,00,000 against Reliance, he would later report a Reliance gain ₹9,360 too small. The split matters in both directions, and your broker's default is not always right.

children.text: Book Value Split vs Market Value Split

Notice that JFS got only 4.68% of the cost. Yet in Lesson 4.2, the special pre-open session valued it at ₹261.85 out of Reliance's previous close of ₹2,841.85, which is about 9.2% of the market value. The tax formula uses book values from the balance sheet, while the market prices businesses on future earnings. The two rarely match.

body.title: Why the basis matters to you

columns.label: Book value split (what tax law uses)
points: Based on net book value of the undertaking against the parent's net worth
Announced by the company and applied to every shareholder
Can give the resulting company a low tax cost if its assets are carried at low book values
A low cost means a larger taxable gain when you sell the new shares

columns.label: Market value split (what the market shows)
points: Based on prices discovered in the special session or after listing
Reflects expected earnings, brand and growth
Useful for judging whether the demerger created value
Not used for calculating your capital gains

body.title: The denominator
body.textWithBlank: The cost apportioned to resulting company shares is the original cost multiplied by the net book value of assets transferred divided by the parent's net ___ immediately before the demerger.
body.explanation: The denominator is the parent's net worth just before the demerger. That is why the split reflects book values, not market values.

children.text: Multiple Purchase Lots

If you bought the parent in several lots, split each lot separately and keep each lot's own purchase date. Take the fictional Sahyadri demerger: hotels shares at 1 for every 5 Sahyadri shares, and Sahyadri announces a cost apportionment of 85% to Sahyadri Industries and 15% to Sahyadri Hotels.

body.caption: Kiran's Sahyadri lots and the resulting cost split

body.title: Complete Lot 2
body.prompt: Fill in the missing figure for Kiran's Lot 2. What is the cost per Sahyadri Hotels share for the 8 shares received from Lot 2, in rupees?
body.explanation: Lot 2 cost = 40 × ₹250 = ₹10,000. Cost moved to Hotels = ₹10,000 × 15% = ₹1,500. Hotels shares from Lot 2 = 40 ÷ 5 = 8. Cost per share = ₹1,500 ÷ 8 = ₹187.50. The Lot 2 Hotels shares carry an August 2025 purchase date, while the Lot 1 Hotels shares carry January 2024.

body.title: Long-term or short-term?
body.question: Meena bought parent company shares in March 2025. The demerger record date was December 2025, and she sold her resulting company shares in June 2026. How is the gain on the resulting company shares classified?
options: Short-term, because she held the new shares for only about six months
Long-term, because her holding period counts from March 2025, which is more than 12 months before June 2026
Not taxable, because demerger shares are always tax-free
Short-term, because the new shares were listed for less than 12 months
body.explanation: The holding period of resulting company shares includes the period the parent shares were held. From March 2025 to June 2026 is about 15 months, so the gain is long-term and taxed under section 198 of the 2025 Act (section 112A of the 1961 Act) at 12.5% on long-term listed equity gains above ₹1.25 lakh in the tax year.

body.title: Older holdings: grandfathering and transfers before April 2026

children.text: Shares bought before 1 February 2018.

For listed equity acquired before that date, the cost used for long-term gains can be stepped up to the fair market value on 31 January 2018, subject to limits. If your parent shares fall in this category, the stepped-up figure also has to be divided between the two holdings, which gets complicated. Keep the company's apportionment announcement and consult a chartered accountant.
Sales before 1 April 2026.
The Income-tax Act, 2025 applies to transfers from 1 April 2026. If you sold demerger shares earlier, the corresponding 1961 Act sections apply. The cost split principle is the same under both.

body.title: The zero-cost tax statement
body.scenario: Farhan bought 300 shares of a fictional listed parent, Kaveri Consumer, at ₹400 each in 2023. In 2025 it demerged its beverages business at 1 for 3, and he received 100 Kaveri Beverages shares. The company later announced a cost apportionment of 88% to Kaveri Consumer and 12% to Kaveri Beverages. In July 2026, he sold all 100 Kaveri Beverages shares at ₹250. His broker's tax P&L report shows a buy value of zero and a gain of ₹25,000.
body.prompt: What is Farhan's correct gain, and what should he do about the broker report?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Original cost = 300 × ₹400 = ₹1,20,000.
2. Cost moved to Kaveri Beverages = ₹1,20,000 × 12% = ₹14,400, or ₹144 per share for his 100 shares.
3. Correct gain = 100 × ₹250 minus ₹14,400 = ₹25,000 minus ₹14,400 = ₹10,600, not ₹25,000.
4. Holding period counts from his 2023 purchase, so the gain is long-term. His Kaveri Consumer cost is now ₹1,20,000 minus ₹14,400 = ₹1,05,600, or ₹352 per share.
5. Fix the records: download the company's cost apportionment announcement from BSE or NSE, update the buy price in his broker's back office if it allows it, such as Zerodha Console, and keep the calculation with his tax papers.
6. File on the correct figures: the pre-filled data in his return and the AIS may carry the broker's zero cost, so he should enter the corrected cost in the capital gains schedule rather than accept the default.

body.title: After any demerger in your portfolio
steps: Download the company's cost of acquisition apportionment announcement from BSE or NSE
List every purchase lot of the parent with its date, quantity and cost
Split each lot's cost using the announced percentages
Calculate the new cost per share for both holdings, lot by lot
Keep the original purchase dates for the new shares
Check your broker's holdings and tax P&L and correct any zero or unchanged costs
Use the corrected figures when filing your income tax return

cards.definition: Receiving resulting company shares in a qualifying demerger is not a transfer: section 70 of the 2025 Act (section 47(vid) of the 1961 Act).
Original cost × net book value of assets transferred ÷ parent's net worth immediately before the demerger.
Original cost minus the cost moved to the resulting company shares.
The company's disclosure of the percentages in which shareholders should split their original cost.
Includes the period the parent shares were held: section 2(101) of the 2025 Act (section 2(42A) of the 1961 Act).
95.32% of original cost to Reliance and 4.68% to Jio Financial Services.

points: Receiving demerger shares is not a sale, so no tax arises on the record date.
Your original cost is split between the parent and the new company in the ratio of book value transferred to the parent's net worth.
Companies announce the split: Reliance allocated 95.32% of cost to Reliance and 4.68% to Jio Financial Services.
The tax split uses book values, which can differ sharply from market values: JFS got 4.68% of cost but about 9.2% of market value.
The new shares inherit the parent's purchase date, so gains can be long-term even if you held the new shares for only a few months.
Split each purchase lot separately, and correct broker reports that show zero or unchanged costs before filing your return.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not tax, legal or investment advice. Section references are to the Income-tax Act, 2025 as in force for tax year 2026-27, with corresponding 1961 Act sections in brackets, and the correspondence of specific sub-sections should be confirmed against the official text. Sahyadri, Kaveri Consumer and the investors in the examples are fictional. Always use the company's own apportionment announcement and consult a qualified chartered accountant for your specific situation.
